tier_reason: Peer-reviewed Bioinformatics article (May 2026, doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag244) whose abstract, checked into the repo as doc/abstract.md, reports Sassy1 4-15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp; the harness (evals/, run_tool_bench.py, edlib-rs and parasail-rs dependencies) is public, but no CPU model or Edlib build flags are stated in the repo and the paper itself was unreachable, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (Bioinformatics, May 2026; repo copy in doc/abstract.md): Sassy1 is 4-15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp and reaches a text throughput up to 2 Gbp/s; for CRISPR off-target detection of 61 guides in a human genome it is 100x faster than SWOffinder and only slightly slower than the index-based CHOPOFF. 'Over 100x faster than parasail' appears in the published abstract only as quoted by a WebSearch snippet (snippet only; not in the repo copy). Sassy2 (bioRxiv, March 2026) is an additional 10-50x faster than Sassy1 for short (<200 bp) texts and 2.5-4.5x for long (>8 kbp) texts; README: Sassy2 2x faster with AVX-512 and pre-encoded patterns 10-20x faster for short texts (internal comparisons).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Sassy: Rust >= 1.91, release profile opt-level 3 (debug info on; dist profile adds LTO and one codegen unit) with .cargo/config.toml target-cpu=native; the Edlib eval is built with 'cargo build --release -p evals'. Edlib (C++) is called through edlib-rs, whose build.rs uses the cmake crate; the cmake crate derives CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE from the Cargo profile, and with sassy's release profile (debug = true) that is RelWithDebInfo (CMake default -O2 -g), with no -march=native; edlib-rs's .cflag("-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release") only adds a C preprocessor define and Edlib's CMakeLists sets no build type. Parasail built from its CMake (flags unstated, striped SSE4.1/AVX2 kernels tried); Ish built with ISH_SIMD_TARGET=sse.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 169 stars, 18 forks; crates.io 6101 downloads (2287 recent, v0.2.6); also on bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs); third-party DuckDB/R bindings (ducksassy)
corrections.caveats: Edlib numbers come from the peer-reviewed paper's abstract (repo copy doc/abstract.md); the full paper, its hardware and the eval CSVs were not opened (bioRxiv, doi.org and the KIT library PDF host were unreachable). The win is algorithmic, not a language effect: Sassy tiles bit-vectors along the text with 256-bit AVX2 lanes over 4 text chunks, while Edlib runs scalar 64-bit Myers/Hyyro bit-vectors. In the public evals harness Edlib is probably compiled at RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g, generic x86-64) while Sassy gets opt-level 3 plus target-cpu=native, so optimisation levels are not matched (not a crippled -O0 build). The parasail >100x figure is snippet only. Requires AVX2 or NEON at compile time (scalar feature is slower).

notes: Abstract in repo confirms the 4-15x vs Edlib and 100x vs SWOffinder claims; parasail >100x is snippet only. Shortcomings to record: algorithmic win (text-direction SIMD tiling vs scalar Myers), Edlib likely built -O2 -g without native tuning in the evals harness via edlib-rs/cmake crate while Sassy uses target-cpu=native, hardware unstated in repo.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: besides the first-party 2018 study (command lines and public datasets, but only 'Intel Haswell 2095 MHz' and distro binaries with unknown flags), an independent hyperfine run in the hck README (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, Ubuntu 20, tool versions and command lines stated) measures tsv-select v2.2.0 at 1.702 s vs GNU cut 8.30 at 7.541 s on the same 7M-line HEPMASS file; C-side build flags are unstated on both pages, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 2018 first-party study, Linux (16-CPU Intel Haswell 2095 MHz cloud machine), seconds, 10th percentile of 35 runs: numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 vs mawk 11.31 vs GNU awk 42.80 (about 2.1x and 7.8x, derived from page data); column selection (4.8 GB) tsv-select 4.79 vs mawk 9.51 vs GNU cut 14.46 (about 3.0x vs cut, derived); summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 vs GNU Datamash 48.51 (about 3.1x, derived); regex row filter tsv-filter 8.80 vs mawk 17.74 vs GNU awk 29.02, but xsv (Rust) 7.97 is faster; narrow-line column selection (86M short lines) GNU cut 5.60 beats tsv-select 8.26. MacOS (Mac mini, 2-core 3 GHz i7): numeric filter 3.35 vs mawk 15.06 vs GNU awk 24.25; narrow column selection tsv-select 10.18 vs GNU cut 10.65. Independent hck README (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, hyperfine, comma-delimited 7M-line HEPMASS CSV): tsv-select v2.2.0 1.702 s vs GNU cut 8.30 7.541 s (about 4.4x, derived from page data; about 4.0x on min times 1.687 vs 6.827) and vs awk 4.993 s (about 2.9x, derived); hck itself is faster at 1.198 s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: 2018 study: tsv-utils v1.1.19 prebuilt release binaries (LDC; the page credits LTO and PGO for the 2018 gains); GNU awk 4.2.1, mawk 1.3.3/1.3.4, GNU cut 8.25/8.29 and GNU Datamash 1.3 from standard package managers (build flags not stated). hck run: tsv-utils v2.2.0 compiled locally with ldc2 'with optimizations'; GNU cut 8.30 and mawk 1.3.4 from Ubuntu 20 (flags not stated).
corrections.hardware: 2018 study, Linux: 16 CPU Intel Haswell 2095 MHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04 cloud machine; MacOS: Mac mini, 3 GHz Intel i7 (2 cores), 16 GB, MacOS 10.13.3. hck run: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-core, 64 GB DDR4, NVMe, Ubuntu 20.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars, 84 forks; prebuilt Linux and macOS binaries
corrections.caveats: The 2018 study is first-party and 8 years old; the author frames it as a gauge of D performance, not a like-for-like language comparison. The awk rows compare a specialised compiled filter against a general-purpose awk interpreter running a script per line, and Datamash was fed through 'cat |', so same_algorithm is false; the closest like-for-like baseline is GNU cut, which wins the Linux narrow-line test (5.60 vs 8.26 s). Unmatched optimisation: the D tools are LDC builds with LTO and PGO while the C tools are distro package binaries (typically -O2, not crippled). xsv (Rust) wins regex filtering. tsv-utils is single-threaded, so no gain is from parallelism. The independent hck numbers (a competitor's README that says it is not authoritative) cover only column selection; GNU cut's 7.541 s mean has a 1.250 s spread. Repo has no commits since 2021-06-13 (abandoned, not archived).

notes: All 2018 Linux numbers match the page. Tier raised C to B on the independent hck README measurement (tsv-select about 4.4x faster than GNU cut 8.30, Ryzen 9 3950X); other task claims remain first-party only. Shortcomings: specialised tool vs awk interpreters, LTO+PGO D builds vs distro C binaries, GNU cut wins narrow lines, xsv wins regex, abandoned since 2021.

tier_reason: First-party Criterion run with public bench code (benches/grep_bench.rs, bench_baseline/baseline_bench.rs, benches/corpus.rs), Rust 1.99.0, the release profile flags and an Apple M2 Max all stated, but GNU grep is a Homebrew ggrep 3.12 bottle with unstated build flags, so the C side's build is not documented and the entry stays C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9 at commit 5094623, Rust 1.99.0, repository release profile: opt-level = "s", LTO, codegen-units 1, panic = abort, stripped; Criterion 0.8.2, one subprocess per iteration with output captured in memory, warm filesystem cache, LC_ALL=C, default thread counts. GNU grep 3.12 is Homebrew's ggrep (build flags not stated).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2 stars; crates.io 431 downloads (113 recent), current version 0.1.10
corrections.caveats: Very new (crate first published 2026-03-04), first-party numbers on a small synthetic corpus (about 1M lines; runs of 4-85 ms that include process start-up). The win is mostly 12-thread parallelism against single-threaded GNU grep: the --no-index mode is faster than the default warm-index mode in 4 of the 5 indexed rows (e.g. 7.31 vs 8.82 ms on 'fn main', 7.64 vs 8.55 ms on 'use '), and the index helps only on the very sparse query (5.41 vs 6.30 ms); every file contains 'fn main', 'use ' and 'impl Drop', so the index cannot skip files for them. No per-thread or single-threaded comparison is published, so no faster per-byte scan is shown (literal and regex search come from the memchr and regex crates). GNU grep wins -rl (7.12 vs 7.50 ms). fastgrep is built at opt-level s (size), not a speed-tuned build, while GNU grep is a Homebrew bottle with unstated flags. Deliberate behaviour differences (100 MiB file-size limit, 15000-byte line truncation, unordered parallel output) change semantics versus GNU grep.

notes: All README numbers match docs/benchmarks/README.md and bench_baseline/baseline.md; GNU grep and fastgrep run identical command lines in the harness. Shortcomings: gain is parallelism (12 threads vs single-threaded grep), index mode usually slower than --no-index, tiny corpus with start-up dominated ms timings, GNU grep wins -rl, GNU grep build flags unstated, 2 stars.
